Draw the 7 isosceles triangles on top of the gridlines, fill MARK_FILL, INK outline 2.5 px, base on y = 11.0, apex above the middle of the base, left to right, tallest first: 1 Everest: base from x = 9.5 to x = 23.1 on y = 11.0, apex at (16.30, 53.47); 2 Aconcagua: base from x = 25.6 to x = 35.6 on y = 11.0, apex at (30.60, 44.42); 3 Denali: base from x = 39.0 to x = 50.4 on y = 11.0, apex at (44.70, 40.73); 4 Kilimanjaro: base from x = 53.1 to x = 64.2 on y = 11.0, apex at (58.65, 39.30); 5 Elbrus: base from x = 66.9 to x = 74.6 on y = 11.0, apex at (70.75, 38.08); 6 Vinson Massif: base from x = 78.3 to x = 85.2 on y = 11.0, apex at (81.75, 34.48); 7 Koscuiszko: base from x = 90.3 to x = 95.4 on y = 11.0, apex at (92.85, 21.69). diagram.render_note: Heights come from the book's table (p.28), drawn to scale on a 0 m baseline. The page picture (p.31) is only roughly to scale: its triangles stand about half a gridline step (about 500 m) below the 0 m level, and on its own gridlines its tips read about Everest 8400, Aconcagua 6800, Denali 6200, Kilimanjaro 5700, Elbrus 5450, Vinson Massif 4750, Koscuiszko 2250 m (Everest about 450 m below its table value). This spec stands every triangle on the 0 m line with its tip at the table value instead. Base widths are read by eye from the page picture (97, 71, 81, 79, 55, 49, 36 px of a 604 px wide plot, scaled to canvas units): the book gives no width numbers, so they are approximate. In the book Aconcagua (2nd, 6962 m) is drawn narrower than Denali and Kilimanjaro, so 'the taller triangles are also wider' holds as a trend (Everest widest, Koscuiszko narrowest) but not for every neighbouring pair; the spec keeps the printed widths. The book gives every triangle its own colour (decoration only); this spec uses one fill, MARK_FILL. The continent line under each name in the book is left out; name and height are kept. Spelling Koscuiszko follows the LP and p.28-31 (the p.32 picture spells Kosciuszko).

diagram.alt_text: A flat drawing of a mountain range with seven labelled peaks, Everest on the left looking about twice as tall as Elbrus, and the small Koscuiszko peak in front at the right.
diagram.render_note: The page picture (p.32) is a shaded illustration with no axis, no scale and no ground line, so apparent heights cannot be read from it exactly. Measured on the page picture, summit heights above the bottom edge of the picture give Everest / Elbrus about 1.6, but above a ground line at the foot of the peaks they give 2.0, which is what the book and the LP say the picture shows ('Everest appears to be twice as tall as Elbrus'). The spec therefore draws Everest's summit exactly twice as high as Elbrus's above one ground line (10.0 and 5.0 drawing units; the true ratio 8848 / 5642 is about 1.57). The other summits keep the page order and the rough relative heights read from the page against that ground line (Aconcagua 7.1, Denali 5.9, Kilimanjaro 5.4, Vinson Massif 3.7); Koscuiszko is drawn as a small separate front peak (2.0, the lowest, as on the page). These drawing heights are not data; the figure has no scale. The ridge outline is a flat simplification of the page's shaded range. Book discrepancies: the page prints Kilimanjaro as 5892m, while the table (p.28), the graphs (p.29), the triangle infographic (p.31) and the LP print 5895m: this spec uses 5895m. The page spells Kosciuszko, while the LP and p.28-31 spell Koscuiszko: this spec follows the LP.
